title: Mentors, Coltrane, and finding the Decatur Street building
summary: He recalls earlier modern players, Coltrane's spiritual influence, the lack of outlets for modern jazz, and how Luba Glade and Jules Kahn led him to a cheap three-story Decatur Street building, volunteers and Eugene Ray's Coltrane mural.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: And prior to that, people like Nat Paralot and Alvin Batiste, Harold Batiste, the American jazz quintet that was Ellis Marsalis and Alvin Batiste and other persons, Chuck Beatty at one time, I think Otis DuVernay. And even earlier than that, I heard people like Ed Blackwell when I was very, very young. But there was no format for younger players to come and learn from those type players. We were searching to develop, if you will, a school of sorts so that a young developing player might get my experience, Alvin Thomas' experience, David Lee's experience, or various different approaches to improvisation so that there would be some sort of chronology as far as what you would tackle or what you would have to work on. And there was also a lack of outlets for modern jazz to be played. It seems like there was almost a hostility in the air for anything post-traditional jazz. The traditional players did not like to call it Dixieland. But that particular type of music was always an inspiration, but it always was reflective of a much earlier period. And I've always felt that the music had a tendency to sound like its particular social times or its particular social settings. So even though I could appreciate the artistry and the musical challenge of some of the traditional music, something about that particular period of time that that music was created was very inharmonious to the 60s, the late 60s, after much of the demonstrations and much of the civil rights movement that was going on. The time called for a music that was much more attuned to where we were moving as a people, not only as black people, but as Americans. I mean, there was a, I felt a harmony that was beginning to develop during mid to late 60s, where all kind of people were coming together celebrating music, celebrating art, and celebrating life in a way that prior to the breakthroughs that the early civil rights movement were just nonexistent in a sense. And my mentor and great person that inspired me so much was John Coltrane. His music was like a healing force during that period of time. And it sort of made you examine yourself and the spiritual and social issues of the time. And it also suggested that we might take music much more seriously than we had up to that point in America. And there were springing up around the country various different workshops and laboratory-type situations where professional jazz musicians were really passing on a tradition and going about it in a very organized, methodical way so that a young person could develop on the instrument much more quickly as far as the theoretical and fundamental harmonic kind of problems that you approach in playing jazz. And just by chance, I happened to play a concert for a lady named Luba Glade, who had an art gallery in the French quarters. And during the intermission, she asked, well, what are some of the things that you really want to do with this music or what do you hope to do in New Orleans? And I mentioned that becoming a little bit tired of playing in the nightclubs, in environments that sometimes the music was really appreciated, but sometimes it's like just a tourist trap and they weren't really that intent on finding out the real depths of the music. Sometimes in a place like the Avent Hall, you'd get serious listeners, and other times you'd get people that would just happen to be there. And we wanted to look for a place where people came to get deeply into this music from a listener's standpoint, from a student's standpoint, and also from a spiritual standpoint. And in my description of what I was hoping for aesthetically, she mentioned that she had a friend named Jules Kahn that had a building on Decatur Street that just might be the perfect venue or might lend itself to just the kind of thing that I had in mind. And secondly, I had no resources. I mean, the financial wherewithal of renting such a facility or owning such a facility. NEA grants and that sort of thing were just becoming popular and widely known during a particular period of time, particularly, I guess, from the things that the Kennedy administration had started. And arts organizations were springing up all over the country. So that was one glimmer of hope. But in meeting with Jules Kahn, he took me to this building that was, I mean, almost the same thing that I had envisioned in my mind's eye in almost a dreamlike state, a place with a little theater in and around, with an open space that might be for a lobby-type area or a gallery-type area in the front or a place where records and refreshments and that sort of thing could be so. And then also this lovely facility upstairs that we hoped to develop later that had what could have been practice rooms and private rooms for teaching and for entertainment and so forth. It had about 20-some rooms on the second and third floor. And I guess it's safe to reveal how much Jules let that building go for now. I mean, it was just something almost unheard of. I mean, to get a three-story building and a French Quarter on Decatur Street. He said, for the first year, you can have this building for $25 a month, which is, I just couldn't believe it. And it needed quite a bit of work. But here again, I feel like it was almost a blessing or divinely or cosmically inspired because one by one, all of the elements and all of the things that I had hoped for or dreamed of were beginning to fall in place. For example, when we finally got the building, we needed a lot of cleanup work and a lot of just physical maintenance and getting it in shape at first and where to get the manpower and how to pay all this manpower and that sort of thing. Well, through some students at Tulane University at that time, and Matt Herron and Eugene Ray, who was a visiting architect and artist that was in residence at Tulane during that time, somehow we got, I don't know, it must have been 40 or 50 kids as volunteers that came from Tulane and came from the community and came in and did the physical labor of hauling trash out, sprucing the place up and then once getting that, getting the walls in condition, spraying the ceiling black, and I mean, everything came together. Paints, supplies were either donated or we played a concert to raise some money to get, say, 20 gallons of black paint to do this. And then I had this aesthetic vision in my mind of how I wanted the room to look. And I thought that it should, first of all, have some focal point as far as central point of universal kind of welcoming atmosphere to welcome all people of all races, of all religions, of all kind of backgrounds. And I think that that was also very closely akin to John Coltrane's influence of really preaching and praying and loving with a cosmic message of people coming together and that the music was like the central or the healing force that would lead us to the creator, to the cosmic. And when Eugene Ray told me that he would design a mural to create this environment in a room, I think that the most that I really expressed was that in the center of the room I'd like to have John Coltrane in the backdrop as the center of the stage, but something that would sort of radiate a glow on and off in the center of the stage. And then I also wanted the star and the crescent, the star of David, the cross, or universal or almost all of the various religious symbols so that a person, Jew or Gentile or Muslim or whomever would feel welcome, felt like this was a place for all people to come. And in the design of his mural, when he first brought the sketches to me, this is, I don't know how to express this other than when I saw the sketches, not only was it something that I had not told him other than those basic things, when I saw the sketches, the design, the way it fit the curvature of the room and the way it brought the whole room into one mind and made the center of the stage and the musicians and all, it seemed like the whole center of concentration for the whole audience was focused toward center and focused toward train and then focused out into these various symbols. But his drawings and his rendition, even though it's down to scale, looked exactly what I had been seeing in my dreams and in my mind's eye. It was almost a photograph of my thoughts. And the more these particular type things started happening, I knew that something very special was about to happen in the development of that, I don't guess we can call it a club.
